newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi cement firms amend KHD contracts.
newsitem.headline: Saudi cement firms amend KHD contracts.

text.p: Saudi Arabian cement firms have agreed to amend contracts with Germany's troubled engineering group Kloeckner-Humboldt-Deutz AG (KHD), extending delivery dates for their plants, industry sources said on Monday.

Yanbu Cement Co director general Saud Islam said his firm signed the amended contract with KHD on August 25 and waived penalties under the original contract, but imposed new ones if the extended delivery dates were not met.
Industry sources said two other Saudi companies -- Saudi Cement Co and Arabian Cement Co -- had signed similar deals.
Officials from both companies were not available to comment.
"We signed the extension contract on August 25 which is an amendment to the contract," Islam told Reuters.
KHD was brought to the brink of collapse this year by the disclosure that executives at its Humboldt Wedag AG unit covered up losses associated with the contracts with the Saudi plants.
It was saved from bankruptcy by a bank bail-out in June.
KHD had been negotiating with the Saudi clients to minimise late-completion penalties and demands for services not covered by the contracts, and to accelerate completion of the projects.

"We were supposed to take delivery of the plant towards the end of the year. Now we have two new dates that carry penalties. The original penalties were frozen. If they meet the new dates there is no penalty," Islam said.
Under the amended contract, the plant should be in production in June 1997 while the entire project, including the building of roads, should be finished in October 1997, he said.

Islam said Yanbu Cement did not have a choice other than sign the amended contract. "If we did not cooperate and sign the extension they would have given us the plant two or three years later," he said.

"Work since then (the signing of the amended contract) has been very good. The kiln production line has been erected which is a major event for us, the desalination and power plants are ready. They have accelerated the work since August," Islam said.
He said the new plant would produce 7,500 tonnes of cement a day in addition to the current production at the company's existing plant of 4,500 tonnes a day.
The Saudi London-based Asharq al-Awsat newspaper said on Monday the cement companies accepted to extend the deadlines of delivery after the intervention of the Saudi commerce ministry.
KHD chairman Anton Schneider had held talks with the cement companies in Saudi Arabia in June.
After the 1991 Gulf War, the Saudi cement industry embarked on an expansion course to meet growing demand in the region.

KHD's Wedag unit won a contract from Yanbu Cement in 1994 worth $258 million. The year before it snatched a $240 million order from the Saudi Cement Co to modernise an existing plant and build a new one. It also won an order in 1993 from the Arabian Cement Co worth $213 million.

Competition for the contracts was fierce and sources said KHD sharply underbid its rivals and agreed to extra conditions that were loaded with risk, such as agreeing to build roads and pay high penalties for late delivery of the plants.
